title: Don't let this man ruin your physique
summary: A critique of Mark Rippetoe and Starting Strength as bodybuilding advice. He argues compounds do not train every muscle, strength standards are arbitrary, time and accumulated volume matter more than reaching numbers, and pure strength focus produces unbalanced, fat physiques; bodybuilders should do compounds and isolation together.
claims: Starting Strength is garbage for bodybuilding; many men who ran it for aesthetics got the opposite result
Powerlifting gurus reject exercise variety, but bodybuilding requires developing the whole body with varied lifts
The bench works chest, front delts and mostly the lateral triceps head; the long head is largely ignored
Squats train quads, hamstrings to some extent, glutes and hips, but not the calves, contrary to Rippetoe
The deadlift trains glutes, hamstrings, lower back and traps but ignores the small upper-back muscles and the front of the body
The big three plus OHP and rows still miss biceps, neck, calves, forearms, abs and the triceps long head
Bracing on compounds does not build good abs; few compound-only lifters have them because the abs are not worked directly
Bodybuilding is not about piling up mass but about who looks best; getting big without aesthetics misses the point
The powerlifter's big-mover mindset is logical for strength but most powerlifters have unbalanced muscular development
Rippetoe's argument that compounds beat isolation because isolation only makes you sore is nonsense
Starting Strength before/after pictures became memes: trainees mostly got fatter and less aesthetic, with big legs and a lagging upper body
A muscle without a lift targeting it will not grow; on squat/deadlift/row programs the posterior chain outgrows the upper back
You can add 200 lb to your bench with almost nothing going to the triceps if pecs and delts move the weight
The bigger a compound's prime mover gets, the more it steals work from small muscles, so neglecting isolation early creates deficits that are hard to fix later
A pure linear five-pound-per-session program forces plateaus, and its only answer is to retry
A 4-5 plate squat does not guarantee big quads; a posterior-chain-dominant lifter may grow hamstrings and glutes instead, while a high-bar squat with moderate reps targets quads
Compounds can be turned into pseudo-isolation movements; for a bodybuilder a variation that makes you weaker but hits the target muscle is better
Strength standards become goals in themselves; ask which lift, rep range, technique, caloric state and timeline before chasing a number
How fast you got strong matters more than how strong you got: slower strength progression with more accumulated volume gives more hypertrophy
A 5x5 forces load as the only progression variable, whereas 3x8-12 lets reps and volume progress and is better for size
Pure strength pursuit conflicts with aesthetics; aggressive bulking is great for strength but can destroy your physique
For a bodybuilder strength is a means to keep stimulating muscle, not the goal; the intent defines the result
Strength training is more instantly gratifying than hypertrophy training because you see weight go up weekly, which pulls people away from volume
Many lifters treat squat, bench and deadlift with care but do sloppy low-effort arm isolation and then complain it never grows
Rippetoe's skull crusher style turns an isolation into a compound, defeating its purpose
You can build a big chest without ever benching three plates
Telling people to skip upper-back isolation until they deadlift 600 lb wastes years of upper-back gains; do both heavy pulls and targeted lifts
Advice starting with just do this comes from minimalists who take away valuable work
Ask anyone who says just get strong: on which lifts? Unless the answer is every lift for every muscle, ignore it
exercises: keep it an isolation for the long head
Rippetoe's version turns it into a compound
targets quads more than a posterior-chain squat
